narrative.overview:
This is a solo operator's ledger, not a SaaS dashboard performing productivity for an audience. Every screen exists for one person doing one session of work: open, review what changed, act on a few rows, close. The palette reads as sun-warmed paper and terracotta rather than glass-and-gradient software — parchment backgrounds, clay accents, sage for things in motion, and deliberately no blue. Nothing on screen argues for attention it hasn't earned; the one saturated color (clay) is spent on the actions and states that matter (primary buttons, the selected row, the applied status), and everything else recedes into warm neutrals.

The system explicitly rejects the corporate-SaaS-blue register — no indigo, no teal, no "trustworthy fintech" palette. It was measured against a generic color-and-typography library during development and deliberately kept the terracotta identity rather than adopting any of the library's generic dashboard presets, because those presets read as anonymous software, not as a personal tool with room for daily use.
keyCharacteristics: Warm neutral canvas (parchment/eggshell) with terracotta as the single primary accent
Two-tone typography: Poppins for headings gives just enough personality without becoming decorative; Geist Sans carries all body and UI text
Soft, generously rounded surfaces — nothing sharp, nothing skeuomorphic
Color encodes pipeline state (applied/in-progress/rejected/expired) consistently across stat cards, filters, badges, and the per-job status control
Flat-to-barely-elevated: shadow-sm is the ceiling for most surfaces; depth comes from tone and borders, not heavy shadow

rules.name: The Single Accent Rule
rules.body: Toasted Terracotta is the only color allowed to carry the weight of "this is the action" or "this is selected." If a second element on the same view needs that level of visual priority, it is a sign the layout needs to change — not a cue to reach for a second saturated color.

rules.name: The Status-Color Consistency Rule
rules.body: Each pipeline status (Applied, In-Progress, Not Interested, Rejected, Expired) has exactly one color assignment, reused identically across the stat card, the filter pill, the per-row badge, and the status-picker menu. A status never gets a different hue depending on which component is showing it.

rules.name: The Heading-Only Poppins Rule
rules.body: Poppins never appears in body copy, buttons, or badges — only h1–h4. Mixing it into UI chrome would dilute it from "considered heading voice" to "decorative font soup."

rules.name: The Border-Over-Shadow Rule
rules.body: Where a lighter design system would reach for a shadow to separate a card from its background, this system reaches for a 1px border first. Shadow is reserved for things that are genuinely floating (dropdowns, focus states), not for routine card separation.

dos: Do keep Toasted Terracotta as the only saturated primary-action color; every other accent (sage, amber, error-red) is reserved for status meaning, not for decoration or a second "primary" button.
Do reuse the exact same color for a given pipeline status everywhere it appears (stat card, filter pill, row badge, status picker) — see the Status-Color Consistency Rule.
Do default to a 1px border-earth-200 for card separation before reaching for a shadow.
Do keep Poppins scoped to h1–h4 only; body copy, buttons, and badges stay on Geist Sans.
Do use the 40/60 list/detail split with independent internal scroll (not page-level scroll) for any new master-detail view in this app — this was an explicit, twice-confirmed user decision.
donts: Don't introduce blue, indigo, or teal anywhere in this system — the palette's whole point is to not read as corporate SaaS.
Don't put a colored border-left/border-right accent stripe on a card or list item; selection and emphasis are shown with full borders, rings, or background tint instead.
Don't reach for shadow-lg or heavier on routine surfaces; shadow-sm is the system's normal ceiling.
Don't treat the resume-editing surfaces' gray/slate palette as a pattern to extend — it's unmigrated legacy code, not a second intentional design language.
Don't add a logo, wordmark, or branded chrome to the nav — this is a personal utility, not a product with a public identity.
